topic: Altana spend-cap enforcement on BNB Smart Chain (chain 56): does it revert in the EVM (T0) or is it a vendor backend policy (T1)?
executive_summary: Altana is T0 — chain-enforced — but NOT in the contracts prior research and CertiK looked at. The spend cap is NOT enforced by KeyStore (0x6572427E…) or KeyStoreController (0x0834Ee2C…); those are a permission REGISTRY. Enforcement lives in the Altana account implementation at 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79 (v0.5.10) on chain 56, the EIP-7702 delegation target, which is Porto (ithacaxyz/account) as a pinned dependency per Altana's own docs. I verified on live BSC RPC that this bytecode exposes setSpendLimit(bytes32,address,uint8,uint256), removeSpendLimit, spendInfos(bytes32) and startOfSpendPeriod(uint256,uint8) — and that eth_call startOfSpendPeriod returns true rolling-window boundaries (minute/day/year all snap to exact UTC boundaries). Enforcement is GuardedExecutor._incrementSpent, which reverts ExceededSpendLimit(token) and zeroes `spent` on entering a new period. So the period field is real and rolling — a capability Rhinestone's ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy (lifetime, monotonic) does NOT have. Three caveats AiKi must render: (1) CertiK scope was KeyStore.sol + KeyStoreCacheOPStack.sol + six files — the registry, NOT the enforcing account contract; (2) no Sourcify verification for any of the four addresses; (3) the enforcing contract's mainnet address is undocumented and the SDK blind-signs relay-built intents.

findings.claim: The spend cap is enforced by the Altana/Porto account implementation at 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79 on chain 56, not by KeyStore or KeyStoreController
findings.detail: Altana's live relay (https://relay.altana.network, wallet_getCapabilities for "0x38") returns for chain 56: orchestrator 0xaf140d0416a994aebb3fa6212b16ce6700f09751 v0.5.5, accountImplementation 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79 v0.5.10, accountProxy 0xc0f16888f4198f53892c53af859f673e23f26fa3, simulator 0x3f5ccc4ded1325340b93d3711fe2aad14f6d5870, funder 0xaf089b4eca94a4b2f51d8f5668cff244f2c6c4bc, escrow 0x4a69f626f38f6be29125a05048d1a47cfd0a7ff2. eth_getCode on 0x4b5d20cd… returns 23,384 bytes of runtime (orchestrator ~9KB). I computed keccak selectors and grepped all three deployed runtimes: setSpendLimit(bytes32,address,uint8,uint256)=0x598daac4, removeSpendLimit(bytes32,address,uint8)=0x2081a278, spendInfos(bytes32)=0xdcc09ebf, startOfSpendPeriod(uint256,uint8)=0xfaba56d8, setCanExecute=0x136a12f7, canExecute=0xff619c6b, authorize=0xcebfe336, revoke=0xb75c7dc6, getKeys=0x2150c518 — ALL present in 0x4b5d20cd… and NONE present in KeyStore 0x6572427E… (8,756 bytes) or KeyStoreController 0x0834Ee2C… (3,609 bytes). The keystore is a registry for third-party verification; it holds no spend logic.

findings.claim: The `period` field compiles to a genuine ROLLING on-chain window — proven by live eth_call, not by reading docs
findings.detail:
I called startOfSpendPeriod(uint256,uint8) (0xfaba56d8) directly on the deployed implementation 0x4b5d20cd… on chain 56 with the live wall-clock timestamp 1787151474 (2026-08-19):

  period 0 (Minute) -> 0x6a85c43c = 1787151420  (exactly divisible by 60)
  period 2 (Day)    -> 0x6a84f200 = 1787097600  (exactly divisible by 86400 = UTC midnight)
  period 5 (Year)   -> 0x6955b900 = 1767225600  (2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC)

These are real period boundaries computed by EVM code on BSC. I also confirmed spendInfos(bytes32) is a live callable view: eth_call with a zero keyHash returns 0x…0020…0000, a well-formed empty dynamic array, so the storage/accounting surface exists on the deployed contract.

The SpendPeriod enum in the matching Porto source is {Minute, Hour, Day, Week, Month, Year, Forever}. This is a strictly greater capability than Rhinestone's ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy on the same chain, which is a lifetime monotonic `alreadySpent` counter with no block.timestamp and therefore no window at all.

findings.claim: The revert path is GuardedExecutor._incrementSpent, which reverts ExceededSpendLimit(address token) and resets `spent` to 0 when a new period starts
sources: https://docs.altana.network/llms-full.txt (Acknowledgments: "The Altana SDK builds on Porto (MIT) … imports `porto` as a pinned dependency rather than forking it")

findings.claim: The CertiK audit does NOT cover the spend-limit logic — scope was the keystore registry only
findings.detail:
Altana's own docs state it plainly: "The Altana Keystore contracts were audited by CertiK, completed 15 July 2026. … Scope was `KeyStore.sol` and `KeyStoreCacheOPStack.sol`, plus six further files listed in the report: the onchain registry that stores session-key permissions, and the L2 cache contract that mirrors them to Base."

The docs then assert those "are the contracts that decide whether an agent is authorized to act" — which is inaccurate for the spend cap specifically. I proved above that KeyStore's 8,756-byte runtime contains no setSpendLimit / spendInfos / startOfSpendPeriod selector. The contract that actually reverts on an over-limit spend, 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79, is outside the audited set. It inherits Porto/Ithaca's audit lineage rather than Altana's CertiK engagement.

Practical read for AiKi: the CertiK badge covers the public verifiability layer (who is authorized, revocation trail, L2 mirroring), not the money cap.
sources: https://skynet.certik.com/projects/altana (linked as the report host; not independently opened)

findings.claim: No Sourcify verification exists for any of the four relevant chain-56 addresses, despite the docs claiming exact-match verified source
findings.detail:
Sourcify v2 API returned {"match":null,"creationMatch":null,"runtimeMatch":null} for all four addresses on chain 56: KeyStore 0x6572427ED530BadcF7375Cf9A4709D8d2b0E7E0a, KeyStoreController 0x0834Ee2C9BdC3E3efF0a2dC34393D4B0e546A555, accountImplementation 0x4B5d20CD8a3927B500540d9BcCDDc27385c9fA79, orchestrator 0xAF140d0416A994Aebb3fA6212B16CE6700f09751.

Altana's docs claim "The audited source is deployed and source-verified, exact match, on all three networks" and link BscScan for KeyStore. BscScan verification is plausible and is a different registry from Sourcify, so this is a gap rather than a contradiction — but it means I could not read a single line of Altana-published Solidity from a verification service. Every claim above about the spend cap rests on deployed-bytecode selector evidence plus live eth_call behaviour, which is the stronger primary evidence anyway.

Also note: Altana's public GitHub org for contracts is not open. github.com/functornetwork holds only relay (Rust), brand-kit, functor-fees, a keystore integration demo, docs, and a passkey circuit — no Solidity.

findings.claim: The chain-56 account stack is undocumented — Altana's published address table for BNB mainnet lists only KeyStore and KeyStoreController
findings.detail:
The "Networks & Addresses" page lists for BNB Smart Chain (56) exactly two contracts: KeyStore 0x6572427ED530BadcF7375Cf9A4709D8d2b0E7E0a and KeyStoreController 0x0834Ee2C9BdC3E3efF0a2dC34393D4B0e546A555. The full account stack (Orchestrator, Delegation proxy, Account implementation, Simulator, Funder, Escrow) is published ONLY for BNB testnet chain 97 — where it is a completely different set (Account implementation 0x33aD2F49ab9f122f5F0FDF579f575724EfF353DE, Orchestrator 0xcb5CEf3C54aa90e9A7ad602A258D3d360cC862B9).

The mainnet enforcing addresses are not in the docs and not in the SDK's config.ts (which carries only keystore addresses, relay URLs and RPC per network). I recovered them from the live relay's wallet_getCapabilities. This matters for AiKi: a user who wants to independently audit the contract that caps their agent's spending on BNB mainnet cannot find its address in Altana's documentation. AiKi should surface 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79 itself.

findings.claim: Trust caveat on SETTING the cap: the SDK blind-signs a relay-constructed intent and never verifies locally that the prepared calls encode the requested permissions
The documented session permission fields map cleanly onto Porto's on-chain primitives

interfaces.name: SpendPermission / SessionPermissions (Altana SDK 0.8.0)
On-chain spend-limit surface verified in chain-56 runtime bytecode of 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79
GuardedExecutor._incrementSpent — the revert that makes the cap T0
interfaces.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ithacaxyz/account/main/src/GuardedExecutor.sol (Porto — pinned dependency of the Altana SDK per docs.altana.network Acknowledgments)

interfaces.name: Live proof of rolling-period boundaries on chain 56
interfaces.body:
now = 1787151474  (2026-08-19)

eth_call 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79
  data = 0xfaba56d8 <uint256 now> <uint8 period>

  period 0 (Minute) -> 0x6a85c43c = 1787151420   (1787151420 % 60    == 0)
  period 2 (Day)    -> 0x6a84f200 = 1787097600   (1787097600 % 86400 == 0, UTC midnight)
  period 5 (Year)   -> 0x6955b900 = 1767225600   (2026-01-01T00:00:00Z)

eth_call spendInfos(bytes32 0) -> 0x...0020...0000  (well-formed empty SpendInfo[])

Contrast: Rhinestone ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy on the same chain has no
block.timestamp at all — monotonic lifetime `alreadySpent`, no window.

gaps: No Solidity source could be read from any verification service. Sourcify returns null for KeyStore, KeyStoreController, the account implementation and the orchestrator on chain 56. BscScan (Cloudflare-gated) was not reached. All conclusions rest on deployed-bytecode selector matching plus live eth_call behaviour, cross-referenced against ithacaxyz/account source. Byte-for-byte equivalence between deployed v0.5.10 and ithacaxyz/account main was NOT established.

The CertiK report itself was not opened. Scope ("KeyStore.sol and KeyStoreCacheOPStack.sol, plus six further files") is quoted from Altana's own docs, not from the PDF. The six additional files are unnamed there. skynet.certik.com/projects/altana was not fetched — worth one fetch before shipping if AiKi displays a CertiK badge.

The exact revert error selector for ExceededSpendLimit(address) (0x9054c912) was not byte-matched in the deployed runtime. Likely Solady-style assembly reverts / optimizer packing, but the specific revert string in v0.5.10 is source-inferred rather than confirmed against the deployed bytes.

Not empirically tested end-to-end: no session was granted with a spend cap and then deliberately exceeded to observe the revert. That is the one test that would move this from strong inference to demonstrated behaviour, and it is cheap on BNB testnet (chain 97, full stack deployed, faucet available at testnet.bnbchain.org/faucet-smart).

Unknown whether Altana's relay is the only path to execution. If the Orchestrator 0xaf140d0416a994aebb3fa6212b16ce6700f09751 accepts intents from any submitter, a user can bypass a censoring relay; if submission is gated, liveness (not the cap) is vendor-dependent. Not checked.

Whether an admin can raise a live session's spend limit without the session key's involvement, and how fast a revoke propagates, were not measured. revoke(bytes32) (0xb75c7dc6) is present in the runtime, so revocation is on-chain, but timing was not tested.

The relationship between the L2 cache on Base (0x6572427E…, same address as the BSC KeyStore) and spend enforcement was not examined. Base is documented as verification-only with no relay, so spend caps almost certainly do not mirror there — but AiKi should not imply cross-chain cap enforcement.
aiki_implications: Ship the T0 claim, but rewrite the copy. "Enforced on-chain, survives even a compromised AiKi" is defensible for the EXECUTION path and materially true — but name the enforcing contract in the UI: AltanaAccount implementation 0x4b5d20cd8a3927b500540d9bccddc27385c9fa79 on chain 56, the EIP-7702 delegation target. Do NOT point users at KeyStore 0x6572427E… for the spend cap; that contract provably contains no spend logic and pointing there would be a false citation users could check.

Narrow the survivability claim to what the evidence supports: the cap survives a compromised agent, a compromised session key, and a compromised relay AT EXECUTION TIME. It does not automatically survive a compromised relay AT PROVISIONING TIME, because the SDK blind-signs the relay-constructed intent. Mitigate in AiKi's own code: after grantSession, read spendInfos(keyHash) off the wallet and assert the limit/period/token match what the user asked for. Refuse to hand the session to an agent if they do not. That single call converts the residual trust assumption into a verified fact and is the strongest thing AiKi can do here.

Do not let the CertiK badge imply the spend cap is audited. Scope was KeyStore.sol + KeyStoreCacheOPStack.sol + six files — the registry layer. The contract that reverts on an over-limit spend was outside that engagement and rides Porto/Ithaca's audit lineage instead. If AiKi renders "CertiK audited" next to "spend cap enforced on-chain", a reader will fuse them into a claim that is not true. Render them as two separate rows with separate scopes.

The rolling window is AiKi's genuine differentiator and should be stated concretely, not vaguely. Altana enforces per-token caps that reset on real UTC boundaries — minute/hour/day/week/month/year — verified live via startOfSpendPeriod on chain 56. Rhinestone's SmartSession on the same chain ships ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy as a LIFETIME monotonic counter with no block.timestamp, and TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit are not deployed on 56 at all. "100 USDT per day, resetting at UTC midnight, enforced by the EVM" is a claim no competitor on BNB Chain can currently match. Say exactly that.

Surface the enforcing address yourself, because Altana does not. Their Networks & Addresses page lists only KeyStore and KeyStoreController for chain 56; the full account stack is published only for testnet 97 and is a different address set. A user who wants to verify their own cap has no documented address to look up. AiKi shipping 0x4b5d20cd… with a BscScan link is a real trust win and costs nothing.

Flag the verification gap honestly rather than hiding it. No Sourcify match exists for any of the four addresses, so AiKi cannot link users to readable verified source the way it can for its own contracts. Either link BscScan (and accept that Altana's "exact match verified" claim is unconfirmed by an independent registry), or state that verification rests on bytecode selector evidence. Do not assert "source-verified" on Altana's say-so.

Before the 9 Sep deadline, close the last gap cheaply: on BNB testnet chain 97 (full stack deployed, faucet available), grant a session with a 1-token/minute cap and deliberately exceed it. An observed ExceededSpendLimit revert turns the strongest remaining inference into a demonstrated fact, and the tx hash becomes evidence AiKi can cite in the UI. This is roughly an hour of work and it is the single highest-value verification left.

Treat spend-cap enforcement and liveness as separate guarantees in the UI. The cap is chain-enforced; whether a transaction gets included still depends on Altana's relay (relay.altana.network, version 26.1.4). Whether the Orchestrator accepts intents from arbitrary submitters was not established, so do not imply users can route around a censoring or offline relay.
